conceptCapsule.title: Kinetic Energy Formulation & The Work-Energy Principle
conceptCapsule.summary: 1. Kinetic Energy & Linear Momentum: $K = \frac{p^2}{2m} = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$. A fractional increase in momentum $\Delta p/p = x$ produces a kinetic energy ratio of $K'/K = (1+x)^2$. 2. Work-Energy Theorem: The net work done by all forces (conservative, non-conservative, internal, external, and pseudo forces in non-inertial frames) equals the change in kinetic energy: $W_{\text{all}} = W_c + W_{nc} + W_{\text{pseudo}} = \Delta K = K_f - K_i$. 3. Stopping Distances & Bullet Penetration: Against a constant retarding force $F_R$, stopping distance is $s = \frac{mv^2}{2F_R} \propto v^2$. If a bullet loses $\frac{1}{n}$ of its speed in distance $d$, the remaining penetration distance is $x = \frac{d}{n^2 - 1}$. 4. Continuous Mass Rate: When mass is continuously accelerated to speed $v$ at rate $\frac{dm}{dt} = \rho A v$, the rate of kinetic energy delivery is $P_K = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{dm}{dt}\right)v^2 = \frac{1}{2}\rho A v^3$.
conceptCapsule.keyFormula: $$K = \frac{p^2}{2m}, \quad W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K = \frac{1}{2}m(v_f^2 - v_i^2), \quad s_{\text{stopping}} = \frac{v^2}{2\mu_k g}, \quad P_{\text{kinetic}} = \frac{1}{2}\rho A v^3$$
conceptCapsule.examTrap: Do not confuse the Work-Energy Theorem ($W_{\text{all}} = \Delta K$) with the Principle of Conservation of Mechanical Energy ($W_{nc} = 0 \implies \Delta(K + U) = 0$). The Work-Energy Theorem is universally true for ANY force field (even with friction and air resistance), whereas mechanical energy is conserved only when non-conservative forces do zero work.

questions.statement: If the linear momentum of a body increases by $50\%$, the percentage increase in its kinetic energy is:
questions.solution:
$$K = \frac{p^2}{2m} \implies K' = \frac{(1.5p)^2}{2m} = 2.25 K \implies \% \text{ increase} = (2.25 - 1) \times 100\% = 125\%$$
Therefore, Option B is correct.

questions.statement: A bullet of mass $m$ penetrates into a fixed wooden block and loses half of its velocity after traversing a distance $d = 3\text{ cm}$. Assuming a constant resistive force, the additional distance the bullet will penetrate before coming to complete rest is:
questions.solution:
1. Work-Energy Phase 1: $-F_R (3) = \frac{1}{2}m(u/2)^2 - \frac{1}{2}mu^2 = -\frac{3}{8}mu^2 \implies F_R = \frac{1}{8}mu^2$.
2. Phase 2: $-F_R x = 0 - \frac{1}{2}m(u/2)^2 = -\frac{1}{8}mu^2 \implies x = 1\text{ cm}$.
Therefore, Option A is correct.

questions.statement: A block of mass $m = 2\text{ kg}$ is dropped from a height $h = 40\text{ cm}$ onto a vertical spring of spring constant $k = 1960\text{ N/m}$. The maximum compression $x$ of the spring is ($g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$):
questions.solution:
Work-Energy Theorem from drop to maximum compression ($\Delta K = 0$):
$$mg(h + x) - \frac{1}{2}kx^2 = 0 \implies 2(9.8)(0.4 + x) - 980x^2 = 0 \implies 50x^2 - x - 0.4 = 0$$
$$x = \frac{1 + \sqrt{1 + 80}}{100} = \frac{1 + 9}{100} = 0.10\text{ m} = 10\text{ cm}$$
Therefore, Option C is correct.

questions.statement: The Work-Energy Theorem states that the net work done on a particle equals the change in its kinetic energy ($W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K$). This theorem is valid in:

options.text: Non-inertial frames only if work done by pseudo forces is included
Both inertial and non-inertial frames (with pseudo force work accounted for)

questions.solution:
The Work-Energy Theorem is universally valid in all inertial frames and holds in non-inertial frames as long as the work done by pseudo forces is included in $W_{\text{net}}$.
Therefore, Option C is correct.

questions.statement: A particle of mass $m = 0.5\text{ kg}$ moves along a straight line with velocity $v(x) = 5x^{3/2}\text{ m/s}$. The work done by the net force during its displacement from $x = 0$ to $x = 2\text{ m}$ is:
questions.solution:
1. At $x = 0$, $v_i = 0$. At $x = 2\text{ m}$, $v_f^2 = 25(2^3) = 200\text{ m}^2/\text{s}^2$.
2. By Work-Energy Theorem: $W = \frac{1}{2}m v_f^2 - 0 = \frac{1}{2}(0.5)(200) = 50\text{ J}$. (Note: for $m = 1\text{ kg}$, $W = 100\text{ J}$; for $0.5\text{ kg}$, $W = 50\text{ J}$).
Therefore, Option C is correct.

questions.statement: A block of mass $m = 4\text{ kg}$ sliding on a frictionless horizontal floor at $v = 10\text{ m/s}$ enters a rough patch of length $L = 5\text{ m}$ where the kinetic friction coefficient varies as $\mu_k(x) = 0.1x$. The speed of the block as it exits the rough patch is ($g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$):
questions.solution:
1. Friction work: $W_f = -\int_0^5 (0.1x)(4)(10)\,dx = -4\left[\frac{x^2}{2}\right]_0^5 = -50\text{ J}$.
2. Work-Energy Theorem: $-50 = \frac{1}{2}(4)v_f^2 - \frac{1}{2}(4)(100) \implies 2v_f^2 = 150 \implies v_f = \sqrt{75} \approx 8.66\text{ m/s}$.
Therefore, Option B is correct.

questions.statement: A body of mass $m = 2\text{ kg}$ is projected vertically upward with speed $u = 30\text{ m/s}$. If air resistance does $-100\text{ J}$ of work during the upward ascent, the maximum height reached by the body is ($g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$):
questions.solution:
$$W_g + W_{\text{air}} = 0 - \frac{1}{2}m u^2 \implies -2(10)h - 100 = -\frac{1}{2}(2)(900) \implies -20h = -800 \implies h = 40\text{ m}$$
Therefore, Option A is correct.

questions.statement: A car of mass $M$ moving at speed $v$ is brought to rest over a minimum stopping distance $s$ by maximum braking force. If the initial speed of the car is tripled ($v' = 3v$) under identical road conditions, the new minimum stopping distance will be:
questions.solution:
$$-f_k s = 0 - \frac{1}{2}M v^2 \implies s = \frac{M v^2}{2f_k} \propto v^2 \implies s' = 3^2 s = 9s$$
Therefore, Option C is correct.

questions.statement: A variable force $F = 6t\text{ N}$ acts on a body of mass $m = 2\text{ kg}$ initially at rest on a frictionless surface. The work done by the force in the first $t = 2\text{ seconds}$ is:
questions.solution:
Acceleration $a = 3t$. Velocity at $t = 2$: $v = \int_0^2 3t\,dt = 6\text{ m/s}$.
By Work-Energy Theorem: $W = \Delta K = \frac{1}{2}(2)(6^2) = 36\text{ J}$.
Therefore, Option B is correct.

questions.statement: Two masses $m_1 = 4\text{ kg}$ and $m_2 = 9\text{ kg}$ have equal kinetic energies. The ratio of their linear momenta $p_1 / p_2$ is:
questions.solution:
$$\frac{p_1}{p_2} = \frac{\sqrt{2m_1 K}}{\sqrt{2m_2 K}} = \sqrt{\frac{m_1}{m_2}} = \sqrt{\frac{4}{9}} = \frac{2}{3}$$
Therefore, Option A is correct.

questions.statement: A particle moves along the $x$-axis from $x = 0$ to $x = 4\text{ m}$ under the influence of force $F(x) = (10 - 2x)\text{ N}$. If its kinetic energy at $x = 0$ is $16\text{ J}$, its kinetic energy at $x = 4\text{ m}$ is:
questions.solution:
1. Work done: $W = \int_0^4 (10 - 2x)\,dx = [10x - x^2]_0^4 = 40 - 16 = 24\text{ J}$.
2. Final KE: $K_f = K_i + W = 16 + 24 = 40\text{ J}$.
Therefore, Option C is correct.

questions.statement: A chain of mass $m$ and length $l$ is released from rest on a smooth table with $1/3$rd of its length hanging over the edge. The speed of the chain as its last link slips off the table is:
questions.solution:
$$\Delta K = U_i - U_f = -\frac{mgl}{18} - \left(-\frac{mgl}{2}\right) = \frac{4}{9}mgl \implies \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{4}{9}mgl \implies v = \sqrt{\frac{8gl}{9}}$$
Therefore, Option A is correct.

questions.statement: A pendulum bob of mass $m$ is suspended by a string of length $L$. The minimum horizontal speed $u$ that must be imparted to the bob at the lowest point so that the string becomes slack only after reaching the horizontal level ($\theta > 90^\circ$) is:
questions.solution:
To just reach the horizontal level without slacking, speed at horizontal must be $v \ge 0$:
$$-mgL = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 - \frac{1}{2}mu^2 \implies u_{\text{min}} = \sqrt{2gL}$$
Therefore, Option A is correct.

questions.statement: A block of mass $m = 1\text{ kg}$ is attached to a horizontal spring of stiffness $k = 100\text{ N/m}$. The block is compressed by $x_0 = 0.2\text{ m}$ and released from rest on a rough table ($\mu_k = 0.1$). The speed of the block as it passes through the natural length position is ($g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$):
questions.solution:
$$\frac{1}{2}kx_0^2 - \mu_k mg x_0 = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 \implies 2.0 - 0.2 = 0.5 v^2 \implies v = \sqrt{3.6} \approx 1.897\text{ m/s}$$
Therefore, Option A is correct.

questions.statement: An engine pumps water continuously through a hose with cross-sectional area $A$. If water emerges with speed $v$ and density $ho$, the rate at which kinetic energy is imparted to the water is:
questions.solution:
$$P_K = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{dm}{dt}\right)v^2 = \frac{1}{2}(\rho A v)v^2 = \frac{1}{2}\rho A v^3$$
Therefore, Option A is correct.

questions.statement: A body of mass $m$ is moving in a circular path of radius $r$ with a constant tangential acceleration $a_t$. If the kinetic energy of the body is $K$ after $n$ complete revolutions from rest, the value of $a_t$ is:
questions.solution:
Total distance: $s = 2\pi n r$. Tangential force: $F_t = m a_t$.
Work-Energy Theorem: $W = F_t s = (m a_t)(2\pi n r) = K \implies a_t = \frac{K}{2\pi n m r}$.
Therefore, Option A is correct.

questions.statement: A particle of mass $m$ is moving in a force field where potential energy is $U(r) = \dfrac{a}{r^2} - \dfrac{b}{r}$ ($a, b > 0$). The kinetic energy of the particle in a stable circular orbit of radius $r_0$ is:
questions.solution:
Equilibrium: $F(r_0) = 0 \implies r_0 = \frac{2a}{b}$. Kinetic energy: $K = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{b}{r_0} - \frac{2a}{r_0^2}\right) = \frac{b^2}{8a}$.
Therefore, Option A is correct.

questions.statement: A bullet of mass $m$ travelling horizontally with velocity $v$ strikes a sandbag of mass $M$ suspended by a rope of length $L$ and gets embedded in it. The loss of kinetic energy during the collision is:
questions.solution:
$$\Delta K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 - \frac{1}{2}(M + m)\left(\frac{mv}{M + m}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{Mm}{M + m}\right)v^2$$
Therefore, Option A is correct.

questions.statement: A uniform rope of length $L$ and mass $M$ held vertically is dropped onto a table from rest with its lower end just touching the tabletop. The kinetic energy of the rope when a length $y$ has landed on the table is:
questions.solution:
Remaining moving mass: $M' = M\left(\frac{L - y}{L}\right)$. Falling speed: $v = \sqrt{2gy}$.
$$K = \frac{1}{2}M' v^2 = Mgy\left(\frac{L - y}{L}\right)$$
Therefore, Option B is correct.

questions.statement: A particle of mass $m$ begins to move along the $x$-axis under a net force such that its power delivered varies with time as $P(t) = \alpha t$ ($\alpha = \text{constant}$). The displacement $s$ of the particle from rest as a function of time $t$ is proportional to:
questions.solution:
$$\frac{dK}{dt} = \alpha t \implies K = \frac{1}{2}\alpha t^2 \implies v = \sqrt{\frac{\alpha}{m}} t \implies s = \int v\,dt \propto t^2$$
Therefore, Option A is correct.
